passage: Neelam, you're starting your first job on Monday, so let your Gargi Masi tell you something. I was twenty-four at the insurance office in Nagpur, sure I'd picked the wrong career. I spent a whole week rehearsing one sentence, then finally asked Mrs Fernandes from underwriting, 'Could I buy you a coffee sometime?' She said yes before I finished. At the canteen I asked about exams, transfers, whether to switch to sales. She answered every question plainly. But what I carried home was one line: 'You ask good questions, Gargi. People who ask good questions do fine here.' I'd wanted a map, and I got one. I'd also wanted someone to believe in me, and I didn't know that until she did.

qa.q: Which department was Mrs Fernandes from?
What did young Gargi want from that coffee besides practical answers?
qa.a: She was doubtful about her career and wanted someone experienced to believe in her, which she only realised when Mrs Fernandes said she asked good questions.

qa.q: What might Neelam take from this story for her first job?
qa.a: To gather courage and ask a senior colleague for a short chat with real questions ready, because both advice and encouragement can come from it.

qa.q: What might Mrs Fernandes have seen in that nervous junior at the canteen?
qa.a: She probably saw someone unsure but thoughtful, and chose to answer plainly and name that strength, knowing how much it helps early on.

grounding: An aunt recalls being a junior employee who asked a senior colleague for coffee, wanting practical answers and someone to believe in her.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out the power at the Kochi office, and Jomon had a train to catch in twenty minutes. Seema had waited three weeks to ask him. She caught him at the stairwell, holding two paper cups from the tea stall downstairs. "Sir, just ten minutes? I don't know if I should stay in quality testing or move to design." Jomon checked his watch, took a cup, and sat on the step. In the grey light he asked what she liked doing on her best days, then gave her two names in the design team to talk to. Seema scribbled them on her palm. As he stood, he added, "You're sharper than you think. I've seen your bug reports." She stayed on the step long after his footsteps faded, smiling at the ink on her hand.

qa.q: What was Seema holding when she caught Jomon at the stairwell?
qa.a: She was holding two paper cups from the tea stall downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Seema stay on the step smiling after Jomon left?
qa.a: Seema felt happy and encouraged because, beyond the names she wanted, an experienced colleague had told her she was sharper than she thinks 😊.

qa.q: How did Seema make the most of such a short, awkward moment?
qa.a: She asked one clear question, wrote the names down on the spot and let Jomon guide the talk, so ten rushed minutes still gave her real next steps.

qa.q: What might the conversation have been like for Jomon, with a train to catch?
qa.a: He was pressed for time but chose to sit down anyway, which suggests he wanted to help a promising junior even in a rush.

grounding: A junior woman, unsure of her path, grabs a rushed chat with a senior colleague during a storm and gets both practical steps and belief in her.
